title: RNNs, LSTMs and Sequence Models
summary: Before transformers, RNNs and LSTMs were the standard for text and sequences. They process data step by step, keeping a memory of previous inputs. Understanding their limitations, especially difficulty with long-range dependencies, explains exactly w
content:
# RNNs, LSTMs and Sequence Models ##### The model that forgot the word "not" A team in Kochi built a sentiment classifier for restaurant reviews using an LSTM. It scored 88% on their test set. Good enough to ship. Two weeks later, a customer success manager forwarded a complaint. The dashboard had classified this review as **positive**: > "I had heard so much about this place from friends who visited last year and kept insisting we try the Sunday brunch, and after finally making a reservation and waiting three weeks for a table, I have to say the food was not good at all." Sixty-three words. The word that inverts the entire meaning — *not* — is at word 57. By the time the LSTM's hidden state reached it, the state had been overwritten fifty-six times by "heard so much," "friends," "insisting," "finally." All mildly positive. The single most important token arrived last and had one update to fight fifty-six others. This is the defining weakness of recurrent models, and it is not a bug you can fix with more training. It is structural: **information must survive a long chain of sequential updates, and long chains lose information.** Understanding exactly how RNNs work — and exactly where they break — is what makes the transformer's design feel inevitable rather than arbitrary. Attention was not invented because someone wanted a fancier architecture. It was invented to solve this specific problem. ##### Sequential data Some data has order that carries meaning. Shuffle the pixels of an image and you destroy it, but shuffle the *rows* of a customer table and nothing changes. Sequences are different: - "The dog bit the man" ≠ "The man bit the dog" - Stock prices, sensor readings, ECG traces - Audio waveforms - Any text at all Feedforward networks and CNNs need fixed-size input. Sequences vary in length — a review might be 5 words or 500. You need an architecture that processes items one at a time while carrying something forward. ##### The recurrent neural network An RNN processes a sequence step by step, maintaining a **hidden state** that acts as memory. $$h_t = \tanh(W_{hh} h_{t-1} + W_{xh} x_t + b_h)$$ $$y_t = W_{hy} h_t + b_y$$ At each step: combine the previous hidden state with the current input, squash it, and that is your new hidden state. ```mermaid flowchart LR X1["x₁
'the'"] --> H1["h₁"] H0["h₀ = 0"] --> H1 X2["x₂
'food'"] --> H2["h₂"] H1 --> H2 X3["x₃
'was'"] --> H3["h₃"] H2 --> H3 X4["x₄
'not'"] --> H4["h₄"] H3 --> H4 X5["x₅
'good'"] --> H5["h₅"] H4 --> H5 H5 --> Y["classifier
→ sentiment"] ``` **The same weights are used at every step.** This is weight sharing again, exactly as in a CNN, and it is what lets one RNN handle sequences of any length. Here it is from scratch, so nothing is hidden: ```python import numpy as np class SimpleRNN: def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size, output_size, seed=42): rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) s = 0.01 self.Wxh = rng.standard_normal((hidden_size, input_size)) * s self.Whh = rng.standard_normal((hidden_size, hidden_size)) * s self.Why = rng.standard_normal((output_size, hidden_size)) * s self.bh = np.zeros(hidden_size) self.by = np.zeros(output_size) self.hidden_size = hidden_size def forward(self, inputs): """inputs: list of one-hot vectors, one per timestep.""" h = np.zeros(self.hidden_size) states = [h] for x in inputs: h = np.tanh(self.Wxh @ x + self.Whh @ h + self.bh) states.append(h) y = self.Why @ h + self.by # classify from the FINAL state return y, states rnn = SimpleRNN(input_size=10, hidden_size=32, output_size=2) seq = [np.eye(10)[i] for i in [3, 7, 1, 9, 2]] logits, states = rnn.forward(seq) print(logits.round(4), len(states)) ``` Note the classification uses only `states[-1]`. Everything the model knows about a 63-word review must be compressed into one 32-dimensional vector. That bottleneck is the Kochi problem in one line of code. ##### Vanishing gradients, sequential edition Training an RNN uses **backpropagation through time** (BPTT): unroll the network across all timesteps and apply the chain rule backwards. From Day 14, gradients multiply layer by layer. Here the "layers" are timesteps, and the *same* matrix $W_{hh}$ appears in every factor: $$\frac{\partial h_t}{\partial h_k} = \prod_{i=k+1}^{t} W_{hh}^T \cdot \text{diag}(\tanh'(\cdot))$$ A 60-word sentence means a product of 60 terms. ```python import numpy as np for factor in [0.7, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1]: print(f"factor {factor}: after 20 steps {factor**20:>12.6f} " f"after 60 steps {factor**60:>14.6f}") # factor 0.7: after 20 steps 0.000798 after 60 steps 0.000000 # factor 0.9: after 20 steps 0.121577 after 60 steps 0.001797 # factor 1.0: after 20 steps 1.000000 after 60 steps 1.000000 # factor 1.1: after 20 steps 6.727500 after 60 steps 304.481640 ``` Below 1 and the gradient vanishes; above 1 and it explodes. Only exactly 1.0 is stable, and gradient descent will not keep you there. **Exploding gradients are easy to fix** — clip them: ```python torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0) ``` **Vanishing gradients are the hard problem**, because there is nothing to clip. The signal is simply gone. In practice a vanilla RNN struggles to learn dependencies beyond about 10 timesteps. ##### LSTM Hochreiter and Schmidhuber's 1997 Long Short-Term Memory network attacks this directly with a **cell state** — a separate memory channel that flows through the sequence with only *additive* interactions, not repeated matrix multiplications. Three gates control it, each a sigmoid producing values in (0, 1) that act as soft switches: $$f_t = \sigma(W_f [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f) \quad \text{forget: what to discard}$$ $$i_t = \sigma(W_i [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_i) \quad \text{input: what to add}$$ $$\tilde{C}_t = \tanh(W_C [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_C) \quad \text{candidate values}$$ $$C_t = f_t \odot C_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{C}_t \quad \textbf{the cell state update}$$ $$o_t = \sigma(W_o [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_o) \quad \text{output: what to expose}$$ $$h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(C_t)$$ ```mermaid flowchart LR C0["C(t-1)
cell state"] --> MUL["× forget gate"] MUL --> ADD["+ input gate
× candidate"] ADD --> C1["C(t)"] H0["h(t-1)"] --> G["gates:
f, i, o"] X["x(t)"] --> G G --> MUL G --> ADD C1 --> T["tanh"] T --> MULO["× output gate"] G --> MULO MULO --> H1["h(t)"] ``` **The key line is the cell state update.** It is $C_t = f_t \odot C_{t-1} + \ldots$ — a multiplication by a gate value plus an addition. If the forget gate learns to output values near 1, information passes through essentially unchanged for hundreds of steps. That is a **gradient highway**, structurally similar to a ResNet skip connection, and it is why LSTMs handle 100+ step dependencies where vanilla RNNs manage 10. ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn class CharLSTM(nn.Module): def __init__(self, vocab_size, embed_dim=64, hidden_dim=256, num_layers=2, dropout=0.2): super().__init__() self.embed = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, embed_dim) self.lstm = nn.LSTM( embed_dim, hidden_dim, num_layers=num_layers, batch_first=True, dropout=dropout if num_layers > 1 else 0.0, ) self.drop = nn.Dropout(dropout) self.fc = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, vocab_size) def forward(self, x, hidden=None): emb = self.embed(x) # (B, T) -> (B, T, E) out, hidden = self.lstm(emb, hidden) # (B, T, H) return self.fc(self.drop(out)), hidden # (B, T, V) @torch.no_grad() def generate(model, start_text, char2idx, idx2char, length=300, temperature=0.8, device="cpu"): model.eval() idx = torch.tensor([[char2idx[c] for c in start_text]], device=device) hidden, result = None, list(start_text) logits, hidden = model(idx, hidden) for _ in range(length): probs = torch.softmax(logits[0, -1] / temperature, dim=-1) next_idx = torch.multinomial(probs, 1) result.append(idx2char[next_idx.item()]) logits, hidden = model(next_idx.unsqueeze(0), hidden) return "".join(result) ``` Two implementation notes. `batch_first=True` gives you `(batch, time, features)`, which is far less confusing than PyTorch's default `(time, batch, features)`. And in generation, the `hidden` state is carried forward between calls — that carrying *is* the memory. **Temperature** in that sampler is the same mechanism from Day 7: low values make the output conservative and repetitive, high values make it varied and eventually incoherent. Around 0.7–0.9 is usually the sweet spot for character-level text. ##### GRU The Gated Recurrent Unit (Cho et al., 2014) simplifies the LSTM: two gates instead of three, and no separate cell state. | | LSTM | GRU | |---|---|---| | Gates | 3 (forget, input, output) | 2 (reset, update) | | Separate cell state | Yes | No | | Parameters | ~33% more | Fewer | | Speed | Slower | ~25% faster | | Long dependencies | Slightly better | Very close | Practical advice: **try GRU first.** It trains faster and usually matches LSTM. Switch to LSTM if you need the extra capacity on very long sequences. In PyTorch, swapping `nn.LSTM` for `nn.GRU` is a one-word change (GRU returns a single hidden state rather than a tuple). ##### Sequence-to-sequence For tasks where input and output lengths differ — translation, summarisation — the standard 2014 design was **encoder–decoder**: ```mermaid flowchart LR A["'मुझे चाय पसंद है'"] --> B["Encoder LSTM"] B --> C["Context vector
fixed size!"] C --> D["Decoder LSTM"] D --> E["'I like tea'"] ``` The encoder reads the input into a single fixed-size context vector; the decoder generates output from it. **And there is the bottleneck, in its purest form.** A 50-word sentence and a 5-word sentence both compress into the same 512 numbers. Translation quality degraded sharply beyond about 30 words. Bahdanau et al. fixed this in 2014 with **attention**: instead of one context vector, let the decoder look back at *all* the encoder's hidden states and compute a weighted combination, choosing what to focus on at each output step. Translation quality on long sentences improved dramatically. Three years later, the *Attention Is All You Need* paper made the obvious next move: if attention is doing the heavy lifting, remove the recurrence entirely. ##### Limitations of RNNs Four problems, and the transformer solves all four: **1. Sequential computation cannot be parallelised.** $h_t$ requires $h_{t-1}$. A 1,000-token sequence needs 1,000 sequential steps, so you cannot use a GPU's parallelism during training. A transformer processes all positions simultaneously — which is precisely why training on internet-scale text became feasible. **2. Long-range dependencies degrade.** Information from step 1 must survive 60 transformations to reach step 61. Attention connects any two positions in one hop. **3. The fixed-size bottleneck** in seq2seq. **4. No direct access to the past.** An RNN cannot "look back" at token 3; it only has whatever survived in the hidden state. | | RNN/LSTM | Transformer | |---|---|---| | Parallel training | No | Yes | | Path length between positions | O(n) | O(1) | | Memory during inference | O(1) state | O(n) context | | Long sequences | Degrades | Handles well (quadratic cost) | | Compute per layer | O(n·d²) | O(n²·d) | RNNs are not obsolete — that O(1) inference memory is genuinely valuable for streaming audio and long time series on edge devices, and it is why recent state-space models like Mamba revisit recurrent ideas. But for text, transformers won decisively. ##### Common mistakes - **No gradient clipping**, so training explodes to `nan`. - **Expecting a vanilla RNN to learn long dependencies.** Use LSTM or GRU. - **Forgetting `batch_first=True`** and silently transposing your data. - **Not detaching hidden state** between batches, so BPTT tries to backprop through the entire history and memory grows without bound. Use `hidden = tuple(h.detach() for h in hidden)`. - **Ignoring padding.** Use `pack_padded_sequence` or a mask, or the model learns from padding tokens. - **Temperature 0 in sampling**, giving repetitive loops; or temperature 2.0, giving noise. - **Only using the final hidden state** for classification when mean-pooling all states often works better. - **A too-small hidden dimension** for character-level generation. 256–512 is typical. - **Forgetting `model.eval()`** during generation, leaving dropout on. - **Training on sequences far longer than you truncate BPTT to**, so the model never sees the dependency you care about. ##### Hands-on: build one, then feel the limit Your practical task is an LSTM that predicts the next character and generates a sample. Character-level is the right choice for learning — the vocabulary is ~80 symbols, so you skip tokenisation entirely and can watch the model progress from random noise, through learning that spaces separate letter clusters, to producing real words, to producing plausible grammar. That progression over 20 epochs is genuinely satisfying to watch. The mini project trains a character-level generator on a small corpus. Song lyrics work well; so do Tagore's poems, a collection of recipes, or Python source code. Sample at temperatures 0.4, 0.8, and 1.2 and put the three outputs side by side — the conservative-to-chaotic spectrum will be immediately visible. Karpathy's `char-rnn` blog post is the classic reference here and worth reading alongside. The assignment compares RNN, LSTM, and GRU with focus on vanishing gradients. Make it empirical: build a synthetic task where the answer depends on a token N steps back, and test N = 5, 20, and 60. The vanilla RNN will handle 5, struggle at 20, and fail at 60; LSTM and GRU will manage all three. That experiment turns "vanishing gradients" from a phrase you can define into a thing you have measured — and it sets up tomorrow's transformer perfectly. ##### Key takeaways - **RNNs process sequences step by step with a shared-weight hidden state**, which handles variable lengths but forces everything through one small memory vector. - **Backpropagation through time multiplies the same matrix once per timestep**, so gradients vanish or explode — clip for explosions, but vanishing needs an architectural fix. - **The LSTM's cell state is a gradient highway**: multiply by a gate, add new information, no repeated matrix multiplication — which is why it reaches 100+ step dependencies. - **GRU is the faster, simpler default**; reach for LSTM when you need the extra capacity. - **RNNs cannot be parallelised and lose long-range information** — those two limits, not architectural fashion, are exactly why attention and the transformer replaced them.
